speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask a question of the Minister of Trade and Commerce. In view of his absence I should like to direct my question to the Minister of Finance. My question arises out of a statement made yesterday in Vancouver by the United Kingdom trade commissioner. The trade commissioner is reported to have said that the United Kingdom would definitely put pounds before loyalty to the commonwealth if Russia undercuts world prices. Inquiries of the Ministry press conference in Vancouver and the reporter from the Vancouver Sun put to him this question:
Do British businessmen put pounds before loyalty to the commonwealth?

speechtext: I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Public Works. I wonder if the minister has any knowledge of the repeated accusations that Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation has failed to provide low cost housing in the hinterland areas, specifically in the northwestern Ontario region?

speakeroldname: Hon. Howard C. Green (Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: C.M.H.C.-ALLEGED FAILURE TO PROVIDE LOW COST HOUSING IN NORTHWESTERN ONTARIO
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday the hon.
member for Fort William (Mr. Badanai) asked me a similar question having to do with the town of Atikokan. I think all the complaints have come from that town. The question asked yesterday was as follows:
Can the minister inform the house whether down payments on low cost housing in remote areas, such as the town of Atikokan, are on a par with down payments asked in larger centres?
Perhaps I could deal with the two questions in the one answer. There are three factors involved in the determination of down payments. The first factor is the loan terms available under the National Housing Act; 90 per cent of the first $12,000 of the appraised value of a dwelling and 70 per cent of the remainder. These terms are the same in all areas, large or small.

The second factor is the appraised value. The National Housing Act provides that the corporation will determine appraised values for lending purposes. Appraisal levels are adjusted on the 1st of January and the 1st of June each year, as a result of surveys of material costs and wage rates conducted in the corporation's branch office areas. Because residential construction costs in small towns are usually not less than in neighbouring urban areas, the amount of loan in such towns is usually as great as or greater than in urban areas. For example, the loan level in Atikokan is 8 per cent higher than in Fort William and 10 per cent higher than in Winnipeg. Appraisal levels in Atikokan were adjusted upward by 5 per cent on the 1st of January as a result of the survey of residential costs carried out in the area late in 1958.
The third factor affecting the amount of the down payment is the actual selling price of the dwelling. This is something over which the government or Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation has no control. It depends on market conditions, the kind of house and so on. It is the difference between this selling price and the loan which determines the down payment.
In view of the rather bitter attack made by a real estate agent and builder in Atikokan on Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, I should like to add the following. The housing standards prescribed by the division of building research of the national research council do not mitigate against minimum standard or low cost housing in Atikokan or in any other community. Houses similar to the C.M.H.C. minimum house, which the corporation is prepared to approve, may be built in Atikokan without basements, and indeed without foundation walls. The house may be built on concrete posts. It need not be equipped with electrical services or plumbing, if such facilities are not available in the community. It is known that this house can be built to sell for $8,000 including land, and equipped with both electrical and full plumbing services.

speechtext: Before you make your ruling, and bearing in mind that there were extensive arguments advanced here last night, I should like to say a few words on this particular point. In my opinion the opposition by this amendment is trying to have things both ways. Hon. members of the opposition obviously do not want to vote against this bill, but at the same time they want to use this method to hold it up and substantiate the position they are taking.
I wish to refer Your Honour to two references in Beauchesne's fourth edition. The first is a page 279, citation No. 388. I shall not deal at length with the facts referred to in this citation, but reference is made to a bill dealing with co-operation between the
Unemployment Insurance Act Canadian National Railways and the Canadian Pacific railway. I refer Your Honour to the last words of the paragraph, in which it is stated:

I would also refer you to citation 393, subparagraph 1, at page 280. It reads:
An amendment purporting to approve the principle of a bill and at the same time enunciating a declaration of policy cannot be moved to the second reading.
We also have the words of the mover himself as reported at page 3553 of Hansard of May 11:
We support the principle of supplementary payments in the face of the serious unemployment problem that now confronts Canada; but we say that those payments given to people out of work to help to keep them alive should be borne by all of the taxpayers of the country and not imposed on the workers and on the employers of Canada exclusively.
In effect the mover of the amendment said that he approved of this principle. In all likelihood the hon. member for Laurier will say that if this were reserved and sent to a committee it would be impossible to move an amendment of the type that is involved here. This is not a case where the opposition contend that there is going to be an increase in government expenditure and therefore the amendment could not be moved in committee. At page 3556 of Hansard the hon. member is reported as having said:
It means a reduced expenditure, on the contrary, and because of that it seems to me that this amendment is in order.
If it is in order in connection with the amendment of the hon. member for Essex East now before the house, then obviously it would be in order in connection with an amendment placed before a committee. We have a situation where the opposition are attempting to do something at this stage, but at the same time if the argument hon. gentlemen opposite advanced last night is correct they would be perfectly in order in attempting to do it at the committee stage. In the face of this fact I would say that the amendment should be ruled out of order

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE RATES OF REMUNERATION AND CONTRIBUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
I followed with interest the quotation from the address that was given, but what I have to interpret is the amendment itself and I think I should give my views on it, perhaps not at great length but at sufficient length to indicate the reasoning I am following.
As the hon. member for York West said, there are a number of ways one can approach an amendment to second reading of a bill, and he has enumerated them. If this one is to stand it clearly must fall within the scope of an amendment declaratory of a principle opposed to the bill. Beauchesne in citation 382 makes it clear that such an amendment is possible. In fact it has been recognized both here and in other parliaments as a proper amendment to second reading. Citation 382 of Beauchesne's fourth edition reads as follows:
It is also competent to a member who desires to place on record any special reasons lor not agreeing to the second reading of a bill, to move as an amendment to the question, a resolution declaratory of some principle adverse to, or differing from the principles, policy, or provisions of the bill-
I have examined this proposed amendment from that point of view, first as to its form. The form of the proposed amendment to my mind is acceptable. There are precedents both in this parliament and in the

United Kingdom for this particular formula for moving a declaratory principle. For example, in the journals of 1877 of the British House of Commons an amendment is noted which declined to proceed further with the bill under discussion for reasons of the principle. Also, in 1933, at page 17 of the journals of the British house, there was another reasoned amendment moved in the following words:
An amendment was proposed to be made to the question, by leaving out from the word "That" to the end of the question, and adding the words "this house declines to assent to the second reading of an unemployment bill which fails to recognize that all the victims of the unemployment which is inherent in the modem system of industrial capitalism are entitled to equal and honourable treatment and maintenance-
-and so on. Therefore I am satisfied that the form is correct. The real question to my mind is whether it is relevant to this bill. I asked myself what the principle of the bill was, and I have taken in answer the words of the Minister of Labour in explaining the principle of the bill yesterday, as he indicated it in moving second reading of this bill, which is one to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act. He said, as reported at page 3537 of Hansard:
The present amendments in this bill will provide coverage for a greater number of wage earners, They will increase benefits and allowable earnings. They will also increase contributions.
With respect to contributions the minister said:
However, there is a responsibility on the government to maintain the fund in a condition of equilibrium and this the new schedule of contributions will help materially in effecting.
Therefore one of the principles of the bill is that of maintaining the fund by increasing the contributions. As hon. members know, there are three sources of contributions, namely the employer, the employee and the government. The bill provides that specific increases in contributions be made by both employers and employees. It does not propose to amend section 83(c) of the Unemployment Insurance Act, which provides for the contribution by the government to the fund of one fifth of the amount contributed by employers and employees. However, the effect of increasing contributions which employers and employees are to make under this bill is automatically to increase the amount the government will have to pay to make up its one fifth contribution under the existing act. What the hon. member is saying in his proposed amendment is that the increased contributions to the fund should be made by the government, by increasing its contribution from one fifth to one half of the employers' and employees' contribution as they

now exist, and leaving the employers' and employees' contributions as they now stand.
This, I think, is where I really part company with the hon. member for York West, because if the amendment were found to provide for a one half contribution of the revised schedule it might then be said not to be different in principle but in amount only. In other words, the opposition asks the house to consider a different principle of maintaining the equilibrium of the fund by increasing the contribution of only one of the three contributing parties, namely the government.
It is a resolution declaratory of a principle adverse to the main principle of the bill. It is not an amendment which could be moved in committee except by an amendment which would call specifically for increased expenditures of public funds, which no opposition or private member is entitled to do.
Now, I find some difficulty, as I am sure all members do, with these declaratory amendments. One cannot go too far with them because they would open the way to an endless succession of debates on the second reading of a bill; but in this case it seems to me there is a principle which is different and relevant, because it is a principle of contributions to the fund. Where there is a reasonable doubt or difference of opinion as to whether such an amendment is regular or not, I suggest to hon. members that it should be resolved in favour of the right of private members to bring a matter of this kind before the house, particularly as their function in money matters is so restricted. When this bill comes in and is debated-and its principles are only discovered when it is introduced-I think the door is then closed to a debate at a future time on this particular principle. If a member is to bring the idea of this amendment before the house and divide the house on it, it seems to me this is the only opportunity to do so.
As I say, it appears to me to meet the precedents and the rules of the house; therefore I am prepared to allow the amendment.
Is the house ready for the question?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE RATES OF REMUNERATION AND CONTRIBUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the termination of the debate on the amending bill last night the leader of the house made the suggestion that members of the opposition were free to vote against the bill if they so wished. Sentiment along the same lines was expressed a moment ago by the hon. member for York West. We are not against the clause in the bill which provides for an extension of payments from the present 36 weeks to 52 weeks, but we are opposed to the increase in the contributions without corresponding
Unemployment Insurance Act benefits being paid out. Even the extension from 36 weeks to 52 weeks will benefit only a very small percentage, approximately 3.5 per cent, of the workers from whom excessive amounts in contributions are being extracted, and also from the employers. In other words, we are not being fooled by the contents of this bill.
For the record I should like to go a bit into the history of the bill which was introduced in this house by Hon. N. A. McLarty, the then minister of labour, on July 16, 1940. This is the resoluton which I shall read, as recorded on page 1647 of Hansard:
That it is expedient to introduce a bill to enact a scheme of national employment insurance to be administered by a commission appointed by the governor in council, and to create an unemployment insurance fund from contributions from specified persons and from moneys provided by parliament, for the payment of insurance benefits, to be administered by the commission assisted by an advisory committee; with provision also for the organization and maintenance of an employment service administered by the commission with the advice and assistance of a national employment committee; also with power to the governor in council to establish committees and boards subsidiary to the commission and to enter into agreements with the governments of other countries for reciprocal arrangements relating to unemployment insurance; with provision for the remuneration of the commissioners and the appointment and remuneration of such officers, clerks and employees as may be required for the due carrying out of the provisions of the act and for the costs of administration.
During the debate Mr. McLarty said this, as reported at page 1647 of Hansard:
The surest foundation on which to base democratic government is a happy and contented people. Nothing militates more against happiness and contentment than fear. By this measure, fear will be removed to some extent from 4,660,000 of the Canadian people.
These figures included the dependants of the workers affected by the act. When the Unemployment Insurance Act was first introduced the entire labour force in Canada under the act was estimated at 2,100,000. During the course of the debate the then leader of the opposition, Mr. R. B. Hanson, gave approval to the principle of the bill, as indeed it met with the approval of all parties. However, he did question the amount which industry would be asked to pay as its contribution to the plan.
He said this, and I quote from page 1653 of Hansard for July 16, 1940:
I have been told it is estimated that industry will be asked to pay $50 million into the fund in a good running year, after the act has come into operation. I do not know whether or not that is a correct estimate.
The then Liberal minister of labour replied as follows:
No. I know that the leader of the opposition does not want to give anything but a correct

Unemployment Insurance Act
impression. That would be a very exaggerated figure of what industry would pay under the rates fixed by the proposed bill.
Mr. Hanson then continued:
I have no means of knowing, of course, but that is the figure which has been indicated to me, and I am glad the minister has indicated that it is an exaggerated figure. He will be prepared, when the opportune moment comes, to state the maximum amount which will be taken from industry to finance these proposals. I think the country would like to have the most solemn assurance that the scheme will be actuarially sound, because if it is not, and there is a deficit, the treasury of Canada will be asked to meet the deficit.
These quotations from the debate which took place when the original bill was introduced 19 years ago reveal that the members of the party in opposition at the time, now the government party, were very much concerned with the cost of the operation of the act at a time when unemployment was almost non-existent with the exception of the unemployable. The number in our labour force has probably trebled since then, and the number of unemployed now appears to be in the neighbourhood of half a million.
I am not opposed to the provision to replenish the unemployment insurance fund, which is depleted and overdrawn; but surely when we are asking labour and industry to increase their contributions by approximately 30 per cent with no increase in the benefits to the workers there is something wrong with the bill. The contribution of the worker earning from $51 to $57 per week is being increased from 56 cents to 72 cents a week. A single man in that salary range now receives $21 per week by way of benefit and a person with dependants receives $28. The present bill does not provide for any increases. That is indicated in schedule A on page 4 of the bill, where we see that the rate of benefit for a single person is $21 per week and for a worker with dependants $28 per week.
By no stretch of the imagination can it be assumed that the bill will benefit labour to the extent that we are led to believe. Does the bill include hospital employees? Does it include nurses? Does it include domestic help? It does not include any of these categories. All there is in the bill is a higher contribution by labour and industry without corresponding increases in the benefits, except that the eligibility for unemployment insurance has been extended to 52 weeks.
I sincerely trust this does not mean that the government has given up hope of being able to introduce a program which will eliminate the necessity of accepting continuous large scale unemployment. Our objection to the bill stems from the fact that the government has ignored the recommendations of the

advisory committee to the effect that any increase in contributions by labour and industry should be accompanied by corresponding increases in the benefits.
I like to go back into the history of this legislation, because it shows the difference between the attitude of the government in power when the act was originally introduced and that of the present government. For the benefit of the house I should like to quote from Hansard of July 18, 1940, at page 1719, where I find the following:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King (Prime Minister) :
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE RATES OF REMUNERATION AND CONTRIBUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: I understand my hon. friend the Leader of the Opposition does not wish to proceed with the second reading of the unemployment insurance measure today.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. B. Hanson (Leader of the Opposition):

speechtext: That is correct. I have striven vainly to understand the principles and details of this bill. Under ordinary circumstances counsel would take at least three days to brief this bill: I have had about four hours. I protest against any attempt to rush this bill through the house without adequate time for study, even before it comes to second reading. subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE RATES OF REMUNERATION AND CONTRIBUTIONS, ETC.

I am prepared to stay.
So are we prepared to stay until we see this legislation put through in a proper manner. The prime minister of that time, Mr. Mackenzie King, went on to say:
In agreeing to have the bill sent to a special committee after the second reading I was seeking to oblige the Leader of the Opposition, who made the suggestion, and I propose to hold to the arrangement made. speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE RATES OF REMUNERATION AND CONTRIBUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I believe that in discussing this proposal to replenish the unemployment insurance fund we have an obligation to go into some of the aspects of the question that lie behind the need for this particular action in Canada. We have never decided, as they

have in some other countries, just when the unemployment insurance fund should cease to be employed to pay benefits to those out of employment and when the national treasury should be used to supplement this type of payment. In Great Britain, where in the past year they have had 620,000 unemployed or 2.8 per cent of the labour force, it is considered that anything over 2 per cent is a national responsibility. In the United States they have had 4,700,000 unemployed, or 6 per cent of their labour force. In Canada, according to the figures for January, 1959, we have had 538,000 unemployed or 8.9 per cent of our labour force. If one compares the conditions in these two other countries with conditions in Canada, one finds we have had three times as much unemployment, percentagewise, as Great Britian has had, and half as much again as in the United States.
When the unemployment insurance fund was set up it was to handle the problem of seasonal unemployment, or persons who were displaced from industry on a temporary basis. During 1955 we experienced a serious unemployment situation. Again in 1957 and 1958 we had very serious unemployment conditions. These percentages of unemployed have been much higher than we considered the seasonal or temporary unemployment situation would bring about when we established the unemployment insurance fund. These periods of unemployment were covered actuarially by the amount of money Canadians were required to pay into the unemployment insurance fund.
This serious unemployment situation does not appear to be getting any better. It has been pointed out that in the March report of the national employment service the figures show close to 800,000 workers unemployed. This is less than the 885,000 reported in March, 1958, but it represents a staggering problem which is still far from solution. Taken as a proportion of the total paid workers in the non-agricultural labour force, excluding employers and those working on their own account, the March 1959 unemployment figures represent more than 15 per cent of those who normally work for others. The March 1958 figure was 17 per cent. There is a decline, but the improvement is hardly sufficient to warrant the belief that mass unemployment is now only a bad dream.
Merely restoring the Canadian economy to its pre-recession level will not be enough to ensure that those now out of work and those now entering the labour force will secure jobs. A considerable expansion of the economy is required to provide full employment. The government's forecast of capital
Unemployment Insurance Act expenditures by private business this year does not offer much hope for any substantial stimulus to expansion in 1959 from this sector. Consequently it is up to the government to help stimulate expansion by a large scale spending program. However, the budget is more concerned with the bond market than with unemployment.
A number of businessmen and economists have expressed doubt about the Minister of Finance's estimated increase of 7 per cent in the gross national product. Mr. Ashforth, president of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, for example, expects the gross national product to rise by only 4 per cent over the 1958 level. The point is that even a 7 per cent rise, which the Minister of Finance expects, will be quite inadequate to support full employment in Canada. Our own estimate is that it will require a rise in the gross national product of about 14 per cent or 15 per cent, excluding the effect of price increases, over the 1958 level to support full employment.
This situation does indicate there is a chance that we will again experience unemployment conditions similar to those of the last two years in which there has been an exceptional level of unemployment, not necessarily of a seasonal or a temporary nature. This amendment we are now proposing to the Unemployment Insurance Act is an indication that we are going to try to build up the unemployment insurance fund by means of contributions in an amount that would be sufficient to take care of any unemployment conditions in Canada. Mr. Devon Smith, financial editor of the Toronto Telegram, writing in the Toronto Telegram of Monday, April 27, 1959, had this to say:
The threat that hangs over our unemployment insurance has its roots in a dangerous mood.
The threat is that our protection against unexpected unemployment is being melted away because we are using the money collected from our industrial workers for other purposes.
Then he goes on to say:
Sound accounting quite obviously calls for a separation of the assistance given to seasonal workers and misplaced or unemployable persons, from the self-help provided by regularly employed industrial workers for their own unexpectedly unemployed.
We must keep unemployed insurance free of any share the wealth political enterprise.
I think this suggestion is one to which we must give some thought, namely the matter of separating the unemployment insurance fund from what might be termed a national unemployment disaster fund, which obviously must be supported from the current revenues of the government. It is not fair, it is not reasonable, to ask people to carry insurance

Unemployment Insurance Act against the type of disaster that is contemplated by seasonal and temporary unemployment, and at the same time ask those people to increase their contributions to the extent that the fund will carry a national situation which is not within the control of the contributors. We are suggesting, therefore, that two funds be set up, the one we now have in force and a new one to which we could bring money from the treasury.
The unemployment insurance fund has dropped from a maximum of $927 million in 1956 to $427 million. The average amount paid out of the fund yearly to take care of seasonal and temporary unemployment could be worked out actuarially; then when the fund dropped below a certain amount additional moneys to bring the fund back to that level could be obtained from the treasury. This would mean that conditions over which the insured workers have no control would be taken care of by contributions through taxes paid by the Canadian people. This is an idea that has been endorsed in the agricultural field, and we are only suggesting that the same type of program be introduced to take care of the labour force by establishing a new, auxiliary fund.
We have some qualms about supporting this particular measure. At the same time we sympathize with the minister in the problem with which he is confronted. We realize that the need for increased benefits is quite evident. We agree that a certain amount of money will have to be paid if we are going to extend the benefits for unemployed workmen. Certainly we are very much in favour of extending the benefits from the period of 36 weeks to 52 weeks. But it is my information that the increase we are granting to the unemployed in extending the period from 36 weeks to 52 weeks will require an increase of 1 per cent in the premiums paid by the workers at the present time. This information would indicate that a great deal less money is necessary in premiums than the 30 per cent the minister has asked for. I should like to know whether the minister has these actual figures, whether he knows how much more actuarially it will cost in premiums to allow for the extension of the benefit period from 36 weeks to 52 weeks.
Second, we would have to take into consideration and be willing to increase the premium to take care of the extension that is being made to those that are now in penitentiaries, increasing the period during which they may revert into their working period from 44 weeks to two years, on a basis similar to that of those who are sick or unemployed through medical reasons. I would think the minister probably has these actuarial figures. At one time we had the benefits extended to

this period. They were subsequently reduced. It is quite probable that it would not be too difficult to work out how much this extension is going to cost.
I would suggest this with respect to this other category we have added, namely the category on the top, and may I say that I am not opposed to adding this category. But as to this category on the top, where we have raised the amount of money that an insured worker can earn to $5,460 and where we pay him an increased benefit of $36, I would feel that this would be an inexpensive category to add. I would think that the higher in the wage scale we go, the less chance there will be for those people to be unemployed because there has always been a tendency for the higher paid groups, those in the highly skilled trades, when they are unable to find work, to keep coming down into a lower paid category where work over a wider scale was available to them. I would therefore think the number who will be unemployed in this particular category will be much less than in any of the categories of employees earning much less money.
I think the amendment moved by the official opposition is worthy of support. I believe that the facts and figures presented in moving that amendment are worthy of some consideration. They have taken into account the observances of the former government in the years in which they had administrative responsibility for this department. It may well be that some of the facts presented last night have not been available to the present Minister of Labour. If so, when we are asking for this bill to be referred for further study I would think that consideration could be given to this matter by the minister and that he could join in hoping that this bill would be sent back to a committee so we would have a better chance of examining this situation.
Over the last few weeks newspapers have mentioned their opinion of the increase in the unemployment insurance fund. I think they have generally agreed that we are going to be obliged to give some consideration to splitting this fund into these two parts, one for which the money will come out of the treasury because of the fact that the economic situation in Canada is such that unemployment results.
In this regard it should be borne in mind that many economists in Canada are saying that we are going to have 400,000 people unemployed continually or we are not going to have a rising and expanding economy. I disagree violently with this sentiment. Certainly we must have holes in our heads if we think we have to plan for

400,000 people to be unemployed so we can have a rising economy. I disagree that this is going to happen. I certainly hope that the government does not sympathize with this thought.
The great unemployment that we have had has not been the result of seasonal lay-offs or lay-offs in particular industries because of automation. They were not seasonal layoffs that took place in the automobile industry. They were not seasonal unemployment situations that developed in the lumbering industry. Rather they are layoffs that took place because of the economic situation in Canada. Therefore I think justification can readily be found for the inclusion of treasury money for the support of this unemployment fund, because the fund was never set up to handle national disasters. These things should bear some consideration.
I think the minister should be able to tell us how much it costs to extend seasonal benefits for these workers-I think actuarially the information is available-and how many people will be unemployed in the new category that we have added to those now covered by unemployment insurance. With this information we may reconsider the position that I think we must take if we are not so say that the best information we have would indicate that only a 1 per cent increase in the premium is necessary to extend the benefits to 52 weeks. If this is true, then I do not believe we can support a 30 per cent increase, 29 per cent of it to cover what we would consider to be a national problem in an economic sense. I think the minister in his summary should give some indication as to the actual cost involved in the various increases.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE RATES OF REMUNERATION AND CONTRIBUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it appears to me that the main purpose of Bill C-43 is to increase contributions to the unemployment insurance fund so as to stabilize that fund and increase the amount of money available for purposes of paying benefits to those who may be unemployed in the future.
However, I feel that we are discussing the bill without having available to us the necessary information. Certainly the last fiscal year was one in which there was a great depletion of the unemployment insurance fund. A great deal of money was taken from that fund in order to pay unemployment insurance benefits to those who were out of work and were able to qualify. Because I think the greatest depletion in that fund has been during the last fiscal year, I believe the figures for the last fiscal year should be given to the house so we may be in a better position to understand what the situation is.
Unemployment Insurance Act
I realize, of course, that the advisory committee under the act is not compelled to present its report until some time before July 31. At the same time I do think it might have been very helpful to the house if the appropriate information had been given us so that we would have been in a position to discuss this bill in a way which would be more relative to the facts of this year rather than to the facts of last year.
Certainly, many people across Canada are very concerned about this fund. Over the last two years they have been able to experience its good effects in time of recession, and they have been able to appreciate the benefits which have come from this fund. In many cases across this land distress has been alleviated because this fund was in existence and because demands could be made upon it. I think no greater tribute could be paid to the former administration than to say that at a time of depression, such as we have had in the last two years, a fund was in being to alleviate the distress which would have been experienced if no such fund had been in existence. I believe that this fund, set up almost 20 years ago by a Liberal government, has proved in the last two years to be a bulwark against the country-wide effects of recession.
I say again that people all across this country, and particularly those who work for wages, are very much concerned about the state of this fund. They want to know how much money is there, and what possibility there is of the fund being able to carry on next year, the year after, and the year after that. And yet, although the people who receive these benefits have contributed 80 per cent of the money to this fund, we are discussing this bill without the necessary information which should be given not only to the house but to all those who have contributed so largely to the fund over the years. As I say, there is keen interest in this fund throughout the country, and why should there not be?
During the last two years, this fund has been reduced by an amount of approximately $400 million. We can look at page 3 of the report of the advisory committee of August 18, 1958 and note the status of the fund in 1955 as compared with 1958. In 1955 the fund was in credit to the extent of approximately $846 million. The deficit in that year was $41 million. In the following year, 1956, the balance to the credit of the fund was approximately $859 million, and in that particular year the credit balance rose by an amount of $13 million. In the year 1957 the balance to the credit of the fund was $878 million, and even in that year the total year's operations resulted in an excess of revenue over

Unemployment Insurance Act expenditure of nearly $19 million. We come, then, to the year ending March 31, 1958, and we find that the fund has been depleted to the amount of $744 million, with a deficit for the year of $134 million. We do not have a report for the year just ended, but it seems that the amount to the credit of the fund as on March 31, 1959 was about $496 million and that the deficit on the whole year was about $248 million, which means that in the last two years this fund has been depleted by almost 50 per cent.
A further comparison can be found in the table which is printed on page 5 of this report. This table shows the balance in the unemployment insurance fund per insured person, and for the year 1950, at the beginning of March, the lowest amount for that year was $216 per person, and the highest, $223. In 1951 the lowest was $221, in the months of January and March, and the highest amount was $249. And so we go right on to the year 1958, and we find that as of March 31, 1958 the amount in the fund per person of the insured population was $177. Or let us look at the amount for March of each year from the year 1950. In March, 1950, it was $223; in 1951, $221; in 1952, $252; in 1953, $270; in 1954, $273; in 1955, $242; in 1956, $232; in 1957, $221, which was the same, approximately, as in the years 1950 and 1951. As of March 31, 1958 the amount was $177 per person, and I suspect that the amount as of March 31, 1959 will be considerably lower still.
I agree with the minister that some effort must be made to stabilize this fund. Some real effort will have to be made if we are to prepare ourselves against the type of unemployment such as we experienced during the past winter. Are the methods outlined in this bill sufficient to enable us to do what needs to be done? Yesterday, when the minister spoke on second reading, he said, as reported on page 3537 of Hansard:
The present amendments in this bill will provide coverage for a greater number of wage earners. They will increase benefits and allowable earnings. They will also increase contributions.
All of us would agree that there are some benefits which will be increased by this bill, but I hope nobody will take the minister's statement as meaning that there is to be a general increase in benefits. Possibly one of the things which the government should do is to look more closely at the administration of this fund. I have here a cutting from the Ottawa Citizen of April 24. The headline states: "Big Loss Taken in Government Bonds by U.I.C.'s Fund". The first paragraph states that the unemployment insurance fund took a loss of $10,155,171.51 on the government bonds it sold last year. The article goes on to say


that this was due to the fact that these bonds held by the commission had been converted during the conversion period. Bonds to the value of $300 million had been cashed, and in cashing that amount $10 million had been lost. I am sure that the people of Canada when they listened to the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) as they gave that tremendous broadcast and reduced financial leadership in this country to television showmanship, did not expect that to happen. I am sure the people of Canada did not expect anything like that to happen when they were encouraged to convert their victory bonds, and surely if such a thing could happen to a government agency it could, in proportion, happen to other people who have money invested.
Further, as was stated last night by the hon. member for Essex East-

speechtext:
Yesterday the hon. gentleman did not accept any responsibility for that at all, but if this loan had not been made to the fund surely the Minister of Finance would be in a position to tell the committee that it is not so. Again, if we were to look at the investment portfolio of the fund we would find many holdings of a long term nature. It is my view that because of the nature of the unemployment insurance fund when it may be necessary from to time to time to pay unemployment insurance benefits to those who are unemployed, the holdings of the unemployment insurance commission should be more liquid. They should be able to be used more readily if they were of a shorter term nature.
The minister says that there are increased benefits and that, of course, is a true statement, but let us have a look at those increased benefits. In the first place the benefits will be increased from 36 to 52 weeks. That will include a small percentage, perhaps not more than 3.5, of those who now receive benefits from the fund. Also the levels are raised and there are added classes. The wage level is raised from $4,800 to $5,460. This will include not more than 80,000 workers. I agree with these benefits but I suggest they are not nearly as important in quantity and amount as they would appear to be from the minister's statement. Surely

the 80,000 people who are going to receive benefit from this represent but a small percentage of the thousands of workers who receive benefits from the total unemployment insurance fund.
The actual fact is that there is no real increase in benefits under these amendments. On page 2 of the bill there is a table setting out the rates of contributions. The first class earning less than $9 a week enjoy an increase of less than 25 per cent. The various ranges of earnings are set out in the table and the increase for the last class is 30 per cent. While these rates are increased by 30 per cent there is no real increase in the benefits derived by those people who are in those classes.
Here we have a bill under which it will be expected that the people who are in the two added classes at the top of the list will provide approximately $8 million of revenue to this fund. Here we have a bill that will ask the employees and employers across this country to provide $32 million for each group in the form of additional revenue to this fund. This is a total of $72 million. In actual fact this bill is nothing more than an increase of $72 million in taxes which is 20 per cent of the total impost for a full year announced by the minister in his last budget.
The people of Canada who pay into the fund are largely opposed to having their contributions to it increased. I believe they feel that if the rates of contribution are to be increased then surely the rates of benefits should also be increased. Thus far in this debate we have heard very little from those hon. gentlemen who sit on the government benches. I hope that before this debate concludes those who sit on the government benches will stand up and give us the reasons why this bill is as it is. I trust they will be able to support the various amendments introduced and the statements made in the bill. I am sure the whole house would benefit from their opinion and I am sure the country would welcome the statements they have to make about this bill.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE RATES OF REMUNERATION AND CONTRIBUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have just a few remarks to make because I believe the general criticisms have been well summed up. We can look at the bill and say it is nothing more than a tremendous increase in payments and represents no increase in benefits beyond the two new classes. The entire purpose of the increased benefits apparently is designed, as the minister expressed it, to build up the fund to a point where it will not be in such great danger and at such a low level as it is at the present time. The added hope or the added carrot is that come next election the
Unemployment Insurance Act minister will be able to reduce the payments and then stalk about on election platforms telling the people what a fine chap he is and that he should be re-elected.
This is nothing more than an attempt to force working class people to pay for the short-sightedness of the government in respect of its economic policy and with respect to its inability to see past its collective nose when it comes to the question of unemployment. It is an attempt to bail the government out of a difficulty which it got itself into. As my friend the hon. member for Humber-St. George's (Mr. Batten) said, it is a backdoor method of increasing taxes. However, as I said previously these points have been covered and may be covered again by other hon. members when they speak.
I wish to make only one point concerning one group of workers affected by the act and by unemployment both seasonal and the type of unemployment that accompanies Conservatism. I speak particularly of loggers who through no fault of their own but rather because of the nature of the industry in which they work and because of weather and the export conditions of that industry experience difficulty.
The act was amended a few years ago, I believe in 1955. Provision was made that where a person had a previous benefit period he then had to have thirty contribution weeks within the last year. There is a provision in this bill to amend this section but not the appropriate part I am going to mention here. It was found in the application of that section that there were countless hundreds of loggers who could not possibly meet the qualifications because of the seasonal nature of the industry, the shortness of the work year, the recurrent lay-offs because of factors other than weather, and so on. Quite a bit of correspondence was entered into between the then minister of labour, the loggers affected and their union.
The then minister of labour, the Hon. Mr. Gregg, sponsored a bill in this house at a subsequent session which reduced the qualifying period from 30 to 24 weeks which made it somewhat easier for the loggers. Although I mention loggers it is because I am familiar with them but I am certain there are other categories of working people who are also adversely affected by this provision in the act. If the minister wanted to do something constructive he could have altered subsection 2 of section 45 of the act to establish a closer relationship between the period of qualification set out in the legislation and the inability of some people to comply with it due to the nature of their empoyment.
Surely, if the minister feels it necessary to allow inmates of penal institutions to have
3574	HOUSE OF
Unemployment Insurance Act special considerations under the act in order to qualify, then he could extend that selfsame generous attitude to working people who for one reason or another do not get into penal institutions. I agree that inmates of penal institutions should be covered. In fact, the minister will recall that he was one of the first persons I called on personally when I got to Ottawa in 1957, before the fall session was held, and had a personal discussion with him about these two particular things: one, inmates of penitentiaries being allowed to extend the qualifying period up to two years, the same as people who are self-employed or unemployed because of illness or something of that nature; two, the question of the application of section 45, subsection 2, as it applied to loggers and to other employees. The minister went half way, but his attitude would be much more acceptable to the working class people if he had gone in the other direction, or in both directions, and dealt with the adverse manner in which the act applies to loggers.
I do not intend to say any more, but I should like to reiterate that we in the C.C.F.- and some of our members have spoken on this-have posed a number of questions to the minister. I have asked for some actuarial figures, if he has them, of the relationship between the tremendously increased payments and the so-called increased benefits to which he referred. The unfortunate part is that the minister did not see fit to advise the house of these matters, which I am sure he must have felt were material to the bill, and on which he should have advised us when he made his introductory remarks on second reading. Perhaps if he had done that we would not be going around and around in this particular discussion at this time.
Perhaps part of the reason is, as happens so often, when a minister wants to refer a bill to a committee he sloughs most of the responsibility that he should have off on the members of the committee, hoping that the bill will get past second reading and that he will not be in too embarrassing a position. If that is the case, I am sure the minister has good reasons for not wanting to extend this type of debate because certainly he would be in an embarrassing position if he started to relate what actuarial figures there are, if there are any, to the relationship between the 30 per cent increase in contributions and payments, and whether that terrific increase was necessary merely to cover persons when they are released from jail in order to go back an additional two years, or whether it was justified to cover the extension from 36 weeks to 52 weeks, or whether it was justified


to cover the two new classes, or whether it was justified to cover the whole three at once.
I submit the minister will have to admit that what he is doing is taking over part of the responsibilities of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) and attempting to become a second minister of finance by taxation methods. Perhaps all the Minister of Labour is doing is trying his hand out. He may move into the seat of the Minister of Finance when that hon. gentleman moves somewhere else. It may be that this is just a sort of apprenticeship course that he is going through to see what it feels like to impose taxation on people.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE RATES OF REMUNERATION AND CONTRIBUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the legislation which we now have before us appears to have two desirable features and two very undesirable ones. I think the increase in allowable earnings is something that deserves favourable consideration because it will remove one of the problems of the worker who is unemployed and enjoying unemployment insurance. We all know of many cases-certainly there are many instances in my own riding-where the worker receiving unemployment benefits has been offered work but he is afraid to take that extra job for fear his earnings might disqualify him for further benefits and then several weeks would have to elapse before he could be reinstated in his benefits. The increase in the allowable earnings will to some extent alleviate that problem and for that reason I welcome it.
The other feature, the two new classes of benefits, I think perhaps deserves support because it relates benefits to people in the higher brackets whose contributions are so much greater that perhaps in the past they have not received a fair benefit in proportion to the contributions they have made. Therefore, in the interest of justice I would say that this, too, is a desirable change.
The undesirable features of this legislation are, of course, the size of the increase itself and the fact that the burden falls entirely upon the workers and the employers. Our chief criticism of this legislation is that the government makes no contribution to the increased payments into the fund. Since there is no comparable increase in the rate of benefit, therefore the benefits which the workers will obtain from this are not comparable to the increased rate of contribution. The 52 weeks extension, to my mind, is of doubtful value. It merely restores the original benefit period which was written into the act when it was first set up by the former Liberal regime. When it was reduced

to 36 weeks I do not think that any very serious disadvantage resulted and I doubt whether there is any very great advantage in restoring it.
To appraise this legislation we must carefully weigh the benefits against the impact upon the taxpayers and upon the national economy. We must ask ourselves how many workers will benefit from this extension from 36 weeks to 52 weeks. In this connection I should like to put on record a paragraph from the fifteenth annual report of the unemployment insurance commission and I quote from the bottom of page 49:
The great majority of insured persons have a good contribution history and experience had shown that in many cases the credit thus set up for an unemployed person when he files the claim was not being used. For example, during the five-year period 1949-1953, although about one-third of all those establishing benefit rights were entitled to 180 days (30 weeks) or more, only about one-twentieth actually drew benefit for 180 days or more. This is illustrated by the following: The average duration authorized for all claimants was 26 weeks; the average benefit taken by all claimants was nine weeks; 90.1 per cent drew only one to 19 weeks, 6.4 per cent drew 20 to 29 weeks, while only 3.5 per cent drew 30 or more weeks.
Since that paragraph contains statistics for the five year period from 1949 to 1953 it does include a period of recession which in some respects is very comparable to our present situation. If we had the figures for today I doubt that there would be any great change in these percentages. In fact, as we progress toward the 52 weeks the percentage will certainly drop considerably and should be below the 3.5 per cent mark. It seems then that we are paying a price that proportionately is too high for the benefits that are going to be received by such a small number of applicants.
We must ask ourselves also what will be the impact of this heavy increase in the rates of contribution. We know there will be no increase in the rates of benefit so that those workers who fall in the category of less than 36 weeks, and they are the majority, will receive no benefit at all. The impact on the contributor, however, will be considerable. Ostensibly the increase is going to be shared 50-50 by the worker and the employer. The worker will pay 30 per cent more and the employer will pay 30 per cent more for the same benefits.
We know that there is no escape for the employee. He must pay the 30 per cent increase because there is no way of passing it on to anyone else. But with respect to the contribution paid by the employer, perhaps in the majority of cases the contribution does not come from the employer at all. He simply passes on the cost to the consumer. Since the worker is also a consumer he will
Unemployment Insurance Act therefore pay not only his own contribution but a considerable part of the employer's contribution. Consequently, the increase in the case of the employee will be considerably more than 30 per cent. Just how much more, of course, is difficult to say but it could very well raise his share of the increase from 30 per cent up to 40 per cent or perhaps even higher.
We must also look at the impact on the economy. Since a large part of the employer's share is going to be passed on to the consumer, this amounts to another tax, and we all know the effect of an increase in taxes upon prices. The recent increase in the cigarette tax is a good example. In order for the government to get two cents extra the person who buys a package of cigarettes now pays four cents more. The same will be true with respect to the consumers who will have to pay through higher prices for a part of the employer's share.
We understand that the total amount to be raised by this increase will be approximately $72 million, and for $72 million to be collected by the government and placed in the unemployment insurance fund the taxpayers certainly will have to pay considerably more. Possibly they may have to pay $80 million, $90 million or even $100 million in order to make $72 million available to the unemployment insurance fund. This in turn is going to have an effect upon the competitive position of industry and upon our position as a trader in world markets.
There is another aspect of this matter I should like to bring to the minister's attention. There are many contributors who will keep on paying as long as they work and will never receive one cent in benefits because of the nature of their employment. It does not seem quite right to me that these people should pay continually when there is no chance whatever of receiving any benefit. I should like to make a suggestion to the minister for his consideration. When a person has paid five years' contributions without receiving any benefit at all I suggest that when he pays his sixth year he should get his first year's contributions refunded. Perhaps a five year period may not be feasible but I use it to illustrate the proposal I have in mind. Possibly the period could be ten years, but I think some consideration should be given to the worker who has to pay in during all his working life and by the nature of his employment can never get anything back.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, this unemployment insurance legislation was meant to take care of temporary unemployment only. But

Division
we are faced now with conditions that did not obtain when the legislation came into being. There is now a distinct possibility that we may be faced with a large measure of permanent unemployment. We know that our population is growing and that our work force is expanding at the rate of about 200,000 or more new jobs every year. The theory behind this legislation is that a man's labour is a marketable commodity. To take care of our increasing labour force we must depend upon the expansion of capital investment but at the present time a considerable portion of our capital investment is devoted not to creating jobs but to destroying jobs. I think the time has come when the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) must try to secure some sort of breakdown of public and private investment to determine what proportion will be devoted to creating jobs and what proportion will be devoted to automation which will have the effect of destroying jobs. Certainly all indications now point to the fact that our labour force is going to expand at a rather more rapid rate than new jobs are going to be created, and this will tend to increase unemployment and to make a larger proportion of our labour force permanently unemployed.
I believe this will necessitate rethinking on the concept of labour because a man's life and the life of his family depend upon employment, upon his ability to market his labour commodity. I think we must ask ourselves what is going to happen when there is no market for a man's labour. This situation may not be as far in the future as many of us believe. Certainly, it is something to which we should be giving some thought at the present time, because if we are going to meet that situation it is going to involve a great deal of change in our monetary policy-

He said: This bill is a very short one and, as is apparent from the title, it has to do with the protection of navigation and of the salmon fishery on the Fraser river in the province of British Columbia.
Perhaps at the outset I should say that the control of these matters on the Fraser river belongs to Canada. The Fraser river was a navigable river at the time of confederation; in fact it was a navigable river a good many years before this country entered upon confederation. In addition, it is part of the sea coast and inland fisheries of Canada. One of the purposes of this bill and certainly an important one, is to prohibit the building of hydroelectric projects on the Fraser river, or of any dam for such purposes, and also to prohibit the placing of any obstruction in the Fraser river except those which may be necessary to be built by the government of Canada in connection with erosion, or flood control or current control. And, of course, the government of Canada does this now on the Fraser river, and has been doing this for many years as the authority which has control over the navigable waters of the river.
Hydroelectric power dams are always high dams and they store a great deal of water. No matter how carefully they are constructed or operated they always affect the flow in the river involved. The Fraser river presents difficulties from the point of view of navigation. My view is that the river should not in any way be rendered more difficult in the matter of navigation than it is right now. At this time the great port of New Westminster is concerned about silting up and that sort of thing.
I can say with exactitude and with no fear of contradiction that the Fraser river is the greatest salmon river in the world. The fishery of which that river is the foundation of an important item in the Canadian economy. The salmon fishery on the Pacific coast makes an annual contribution of $80 million to the Canadian economy. Of course, the fishery on the Fraser river itself is only part of this industry and the great feature of the Fraser river is the run of the Pacific salmon. We must also consider the wages earned by the fishermen and all the collateral matters of commerce such as fishing boats which are expensive, their engines and equipment, nets and so forth.

The Pacific salmon industry gives Canada an important position in the export market of canned salmon, particularly in the United Kingdom. This is a prestige export for Canada because Pacific salmon is the finest canned product of the sea to be found anywhere in the world. One might say I have dealt with the economic side of things and all of these factors are highly important today. In addition we must recognize that this industry provides a great source of protein food. My suggestion is that we cannot take any chances of doing possible damage to that industry because of the vast amount of food it produces each year.
I know there are those who say that power and salmon can exist together on the Fraser. That has been said on previous occasions by learned engineers, professors, biologists and others in connection with the Columbia river just south on the Pacific coast which flows into the sea between the states of Washington and Oregon. Expert opinion was that the Bonneville dam could be built without damage to the fishery but that dam ruined the entire fishery on the Columbia river which was second in importance only to that on the Fraser.
There is a canal in connection with the Bonneville dam and one learned gentleman said that the salmon would follow a ship into the lock and go out the other side when the ship passed through, but the Pacific salmon does not operate in that fashion. While I have every respect for the expert opinion of these engineers, professors and others, when it comes to an innate knowledge of the spawning habits of the Pacific salmon I have more respect for the knowledge of the fish.
At the present time there exist no safe or accepted method of passing fish up and down the river to the sea. Getting them up is not as difficult as getting them down. The little fingerlings, as they are called, are not strong when they go down to the salt water. They suffer injury dropping over the dam or passing through the turbines and are killed by the millions.
Furthermore it should be noted that there is no need for the development of electric power on the Fraser river. We have the Columbia river in British Columbia about which most hon. members in this house know because it has been in the news a great deal. Another important river is the Peace river. In my opinion these two great rivers are capable of generating all the power needed in the foreseeable future. We also have the potential of atomic power.
I should like to read the views of the president of the Fisheries Association of British Columbia as set out in a letter to

me dated February 11, 1959. I am sure that most hon. members opposite will remember very well the Hon. James Sinclair, president of this association. He stated:
The stand of the Fisheries Association has been that we can have both fish and power in British Columbia. Fish from the Fraser and power from non-salmon streams, such as the Peace and the Columbia. In addition, there are ever increasing thermal sources of power now available in British Columbia with the completion of the oil and gas lines to the coast. The British Columbia Electric has already built a 75,000 KW gas turbine at Port Mann and is now building a very large thermal plant at loco which can use either oil or gas. The first unit of this plant will be 300,000 kilowatts and its final capacity 1 million kilowatts. This latter figure equals the total production of the British Columbia Electric system today from all sources. These plants certainly would not be built if the cost of thermal power was not pretty close to the cost of hydro power.
There has been remarkable increase in the efficiency of thermal plants in recent years.
The third alternative source of power comes from nuclear energy. In this field, the British are the leaders with six plants either in production or under construction. Two plants have been producing power for the commercial grid for over a year. Sir John Cockcroft, head of the British Atomic Energy Commission has announced that by 1962 power from nuclear plants will be competitive with conventional power plants and by 1982 will be half the cost of conventional power. In view of the enormous resources of uranium which Canada is fortunate enough to possess, it would be the height of folly to dam the Fraser when other such sources of power are available for if the Fraser is dammed, the salmon resource will be lost forever.
That is the considered view of a fisheries expert. The parliament of Canada can settle this question once and for all. We have in Canada the greatest salmon river in the world that provides a vast source of food. There is no need for generating power on this river when other alternatives exist.
In closing let me urge hon. members to give this matter sympathetic consideration. Let us take no risk in using the Fraser river for the purpose of providing power. I ask all hon. members to assist in the protection of our vital salmon fishery through giving their support to this bill.

maintopic: LEGISLATION TO SAFEGUARD NAVIGATION AND FISHERIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to take this opportunity of congratulating the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. McPhillips) for so ably presenting a case with which I am quite frankly in disagreement although familiar with. It is not many months since the day when discussions on this subject were held at considerable length with the gentleman whom the hon. member has quoted so widely in defence of Bill No. C-23, the Hon. James Sinclair, as an outstanding fisheries authority.
I wish to make myself quite clear, as I have on many occasions on the platform, with this
Fraser River Fisheries
authority in matters having to do with Canada's fisheries. I, like thousands of British Columbians, have not at any time encouraged a program which would deny to anyone a benefit. I wish to make that most profoundly clear; but I do, Mr. Speaker, take violent issue with a bill of this kind which in effect does not only close the door but slams the door in the face of all practical and logical study and investigation which could, if properly carried out, be the means of seeing that the people of British Columbia were favoured with both the benefits of salmon fisheries as well as of low-cost power. This would aid them, not only in their industrial and commercial uses, but would lessen a burden on the thousands of homes and families in the greater metropolitan complex area from which I come.
In saying this I wish to emphasize most definitely that the domestic bills for power today, essential to the life of the modern communities, in the greater Vancouver area run almost twice, and in certain specific instances three times, the cost borne by householders elsewhere in any other communities in this dominion of ours. I think before we slam a door in the face of a proper, logical and reasoned approach, which may bring a solution to this complex problem, we should give a little thought to the interests of the thousands of people who today are paying through the nose because insufficient research and insufficient study has been carried on. Too many authorities have grown up, authorities, which I wish to emphasize most forcefully, when it comes to power matters in British Columbia today, believe you should go to see the fisheries experts on power matters. You should go and talk to the president of the B. C. fish association; you should go and talk to the fisheries biologists; if you want the answers to power problems. That is the place to get your answers. I am likewise equally critical when, if you want solutions today to biological fish problems in our province, you go to the power authorities.
I have read evidence which has been presented to committees from time to time during this session. I refer to the committee on mines, forests and waters and also the committee on marine and fisheries. It is pointed out, as I say, if you wish an expert on fisheries you go to the opposite side of the pole. If you want to consult an expert on hydro matters you go to the fish people. It is high time that this whole problem was made free of all closed, bigoted views. Intelligent men, qualified people, must be brought in to solve this problem and must be adequately financed. It is high time, Mr. Speaker, that this dominion of ours started to call on the

Fraser River Fisheries
United States under the international North Pacific fisheries treaty to pay its share because it takes half of the harvest of the salmon that spawn on the upper stretches of the Fraser river. I contend that our United States neighbour, taking that advantage, has not produced according to the treaty nor in any way cooperated toward a logical solution to this matter.
I hold in my hand what I consider to be a very well thought out editorial from the Vancouver Sun of February 17, 1958. It reads in part as follows:
Research can find a way to have hoth salmon and hydroelectric development of the Fraser river.
But the research isn't being done.
Again this sensible warning comes. When will it sink in with politicians who posture so eagerly as saviours of the salmon from the wicked hydro barons? When will it sink in with fishing interests who applaud the politicians and try to sell the idea that hydro soon won't be important? And with hydro interests who face having to inflict higher costs on the public unless the Fraser is used.
I also hold in my hand a mail-out that every householder of the lower mainland received last year. This indicates another expense of modern day costs in raising a family. It indicates that household electric rates must be increased, and the people of the lower mainland of British Columbia know the results.
In discussing this matter there is also a great tendency to overlook a few of the facts. Flood danger is an ever present one on the Fraser river. I admit that the proposer of this bill will say that the bill in no way precludes solution of flood problems. I would like to read from the interim report of the Fraser river board, dated June, 1956. In part, it says:
Since then, in 1950, 1954 and again in 1955 the river rose above the 20-foot level at the Mission bridge, the danger mark prior to dike reconstruction in 1949. However, the system of dikes as reconstructed since the 1948 flood, contained the freshets and only very minor local damage or inconvenience has resulted.
Then it goes on to refer to other very disastrous floods which the people of the lower mainland of British Columbia have learned through the years to live with. The important fact is that this same report in its findings recommends-and I would point out that on that board as one of the five members was a representative from the department of water resources branch, Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources, Mr. T. M. Patterson; from the Department of Fisheries there was the chief supervisor of fisheries, Pacific area, Mr. A. J. Whitmore-that a multi-purpose project should be undertaken to control floods. The reason they recommend multi-purpose projects is that damming for the sole purpose of
[Mr. Payne.l
controlling flood waters in the Fraser river is not economically feasible unless benefits can be gained by virtue of the production of power, by virtue of the reclamation of land through moving siltage up on to the flat lands and moving water on to the surface. I point this out, Mr. Speaker, but not to suggest that this parliament can go forward on such a project today. I do not think any person in the province of British Columbia contends that this matter of salmon and power can be solved today; but we do contend that it will never be solved if we are going to face a lack of co-operative effort and approach the problem on a level of bigotry.
I should like now to refer to a statement by the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. MacLean). I will say to him that I have heard this statement made on many platforms by other past ministers of fisheries. At page 100 of the proceedings and evidence of the standing committee on marine and fisheries of April 23, 1959, the minister said in answer to a question, and the proposer of this motion concurred in these remarks in his earlier statement:
That power development from hydro sources, or even from the common types of thermal development, may be a passing thing. It is quite likely that in the very near future it will be economically feasible to produce power from atomic energy.
It is statements of this nature by fisheries people speaking on technical matters regarding energy and generation of power that wash out a solution of the problems that we are now concerned with. I am deeply concerned with the power cost that results, from this approach. The burden is placed on our homeowner. I should like to refer to the minutes of proceedings and evidence, No. 11, of the standing committee on mines, forests and waters, April 7, 1959, wherein perhaps the most outstanding Canadian authority on atomic matters, Dr. John Convey, director of the mines branch, Department of Mines and Technical Surveys, gives his testimony as found on page 261 and on following page. He had this to say:
Mr. Chairman and gentlemen: I am somewhat on the spot, but since I reported to you almost 12 months ago, I am in a position to give evidence that there has been a lot of experimental work done in the field of the development of nuclear power. However, it is still in the experimental stage and there do not exist any economical kilowatts produced by atomic reactors today. At Geneva last fall it was reported there were some 13 power reactors producing power, but none of them economically. Eight of these exist in the United States, one in the U.S.S.R. and three in Great Britain. The situation is still one in which you have a combination of three main factors: the nuclear fuel, the moderator and the coolant.
He goes on to say:
Quite a number of experiments are under way at the present time, but the cost of producing power for these reactors is certainly nowhere in

the neighbourhood of six mills. There are educated guesses as to when it will break through, but as far as I know at the present time it is merely a guess to say that by 1970 we will be producing economic power.
He goes on at great length and makes this final statement:
So I would say right now that experimental work in reactors has not reached a stage wherein one could give an honest guess as to just when it will break through; and I cannot see it breaking through at least for another two decades.
I and the thousands, I say advisedly, who feel as I do and for whom I speak in the house do not say that atomic power may not be the only economic means of generating power requirements in the future. We do not say that dams are essential on the Fraser river. We do say that, at the moment, the only economic means of generating power is through hydro development, and as long as that situation exists let us not, by passing Bill No. C-23, close the door to a logical, reasoned and intelligent approach to this problem which faces all in the lower mainland of British Columbia. Rather, let us get on with an intelligent, reasoned research program so that we will not deny the people of our province those benefits which may be derived through a logical, proper approach to the problem.

Mr. Speaker, I want to have a few words to say on this, shall I say, most novel and interesting bill. I fully appreciate the concern of the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. Mc-Phillips) with regard to preserving the salmon fishing resources of the Pacific coast but I think he has taken a rather unusual way to do that. In my opinion there are several sound reasons why the bill should not be passed by the house. I respect fully the sincere intention of the hon. member to protect this fisheries resource about which he is so concerned.
First of all, the bill is very final. It slams the door. It reminds me of an occasion about 60 years ago when my father wanted to stop me skating on Sundays and in order to do so he chopped up my boots and skates.
