It was a very final act but within a week or so my father ended up by having to buy me new boots and skates. This bill is final. Section one provides:
No hydroelectric power shall be generated in the Fraser river in the province of British Columbia, nor shall any dam, weir or other obstruction to navigation or to the spawning run of the Pacific salmon, be constructed in or over the said river.
Fraser River Fisheries
If the bill should pass it would finalize the situation so far as the Fraser is concerned. I think the bill overlooks possible developments of the future. We are not in a position to say today that it will not be possible to have fish and power on the Columbia as a result of research. Today I was reading of the tremendous advance made in that direction in the Soviet union, according to a report in the newspapers, where they claim that they have been able to develop power and preserve fishery resources at the same time. It is only a newspaper report but I suspect there is some foundation of fact in it.
In adopting the bill we would be closing the door to possible developments of the future through research and so on. I am sure that all thinking people in British Columbia are concerned about the preservation of the fishery resources but the people who think and take a long point of view do not want parliament to take any action that would prevent any future development as a result of advances in science and in our knowledge of these matters.
There is a second reason for my opposition to the bill. The member realizes there are other, shall I say, surrounding aspects to this question that I do not want to go into in detail at this time, but if the bill were to pass it would preclude the more efficient development and use by Canadians of the surplus waters of the Columbia in the future. In that connection we are not certain what the possibilities are and what the circumstances will be, but the bill would preclude Canadians from using the surplus waters of the Columbia in the years to come in the most efficient way and in the best interests of the people of British Columbia.
For these reasons, Mr. Speaker, I take strong exception to the bill and trust it will not be passed by the house. I think we would be much wiser to leave ourselves the opportunity to take whatever course we see fit to take in the future with respect to the development of the Fraser and the utilization of the surplus waters of the Columbia in the light of the fact that at the present time, as St. Paul says, and I use his words in connection with this problem: "We see as in a glass darkly."

Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak I must say at the outset that I disagree violently with the preceding two speakers, especially the hon. member for Coast-Capilano (Mr. Payne) who, incidentally, is my roommate. He took exception to the fact that the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. McPhillips) in his bill was slamming the door but I feel that the door

Fraser River Fisheries
was not slammed tightly enough or perhaps was slammed too violently so that it sprung open. Contrary to the opinion expressed by the hon. member for Coast-Capilano, I believe that the legislation does not go far enough. The hon. member for Victoria (B.C.) has provided in his bill that no hydroelectric power dam shall be constructed on the Fraser river. In the second paragraph of the hon. member's bill he allows the federal government a certain amount of leeway with respect to flood control, navigation and so on, and I think that perhaps this is one of the difficulties in the bill.
In recent testimony before the marine and fisheries committee, the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. MacLean) pointed out very clearly the sensitivity of spawning fish to any interference with their natural habitat. I, myself, am rather leery as to any interference by power dams or flood control dams. If I may, I should like to quote what the minister says on page 11 of the proceedings of the marine and fisheries committee:
In British Columbia and the Yukon we have been concerned with the continuing problem of overcoming the effects of industrial developments on the major salmon runs. I might say in this connection, in a general way, that one of the problems of conservation is of course the impact of civilization and industrialization on the environment in which fish live. There are very severe changes which follow industrialization and settlement in a natural habitat which may not be apparent to the casual observer, but which the fish are very much aware of. I am referring to such things as changes in the fluctuation of run-off, water temperatures and many other things along this line of which the casual observer is not aware. These things include siltation of spawning beds and the reduction of the sunlight in water by siltation, and contamination and suspension of fine material in the streams, which cuts off the sunlight and reduces the growth of micro-organisms in the streams, on which the fish feed, especially in the early stages of their growth.
Perhaps the fisheries committee, in its recommendations, Mr. Speaker, expresses more truly the principle which the hon. member for Victoria (B.C.) is trying to enunciate. In their conclusions on page 85 of the committee's report we find this:
Your committee expresses the opinion that no dams should be built on the Fraser river, or any of its tributaries, where such dams will, in the opinion of the Minister of Fisheries, interfere with, or be detrimental to anadromous fish runs.
The hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) expressed concern about the fact that this legislation was final. He seems to forget that parliament can, in the next day or even next year, should changes be required, introduce other legislation to replace this legislation. I would say, therefore, that the difficulties in connection with shutting the door are perhaps theoretical and only for

the time being. I believe the door should very definitely be slammed.
What is the reason for this interest on the part of power companies in British Columbia? British Columbia has a power potential of some 25 million horsepower. In this connection, the Fraser river has a power potential of approximately 7 million horsepower. I contend, that we have two other rivers, the Columbia river with a potential horsepower of 3 million and the Peace river which has another 4 million potential horsepower. In addition, we have thermal power, for example, such as that which exists at Port Moody. I believe there are some six nuclear power stations which have been established in the United Kingdom. It is purely the monetary and economic considerations which urge these interests to establish a power dam on the Fraser river because of its closeness to the settled mainland area.
I feel, Mr. Speaker, that of more importance than dams and electricity is the fact that we have a tremendous resource which, in the past year, had a landed value to the fishermen of some $37 million. The market value would probably be considerably more than that. This represents almost 15 million fish going up the Fraser river. I feel that when we have this natural resource that comes back year after year it is extremely important that we do nothing to jeopardize the continuity of this particular run. One of the suggestions that is frequently made in connection with this fish and power problem is the idea of having fish hatcheries. The experience of those in the hatchery business has been that the fish leaving the hatchery are extremely vulnerable. The fish can be produced in the hatchery, but once they get clear of the hatchery they tend to die off in large numbers. Experiments have shown there is no advantage in artificial over natural propagation in this respect.
The sockeye salmon, which is the one with which we are most concerned in the Fraser river, apparently has proven the least suitable for hatchery culture. For example, I should like to cite from the B. C. Professional Engineer of March, 1959 an article entitled "Artificial Propagation is Not the Answer". This particular article, dealing with the problem of raising young fish in a hatchery, states:
A modern salmon hatchery capable of rearing 2 million sockeye to seagoing size costs approximately $1 million and at least $60,000 annually for operation. The Adams river run alone would require 100 such hatcheries to equal the natural production of seaward migrants. The super-hatchery installation required would have 16,000 standard-size rearing ponds, an inflow of several thousand c.f.s. and a labour force of over 2,000. Other lesser runs

which are concurrent with the Adams run would require additional space. Even with all this effort to duplicate the numbers that would be produced naturally, the low survival rate of the hatchery-raised fish would fail to duplicate the natural return of adults.
To summarize, the Fraser fish-power problem centres around the sockeye salmon, the species of salmon which is least adaptable to hatchery culture on any scale, and which occurs in such abundance in the Fraser river that hatchery and rearing facilities are inconceivable.
Two of the greatest difficulties with regard to the problem of the fish migrating upstream is, first of all, the delay and second the problem of transporting them over the spillways. Again I should like to refer to the same article because it very succinctly and concisely sets forth the problems:
Basically there are two problems on the Fraser for which no satisfactory solution has been found. First, sockeye salmon will not tolerate delay in upstream migration and there is no known system for transportation of large numbers of adult salmon over a dam without delay. The problem is not primarily one of engineering. Fishways or lifts, locks or pumps, tank trucks or trains can all be engineered to accommodate large numbers of fish, although the cost would be high. The difficulty lies in convincing the fish that the facilities are designed for their benefit, i.e., getting the fish to go into them without delay and to proceed through them without stress or panic. The answer to these problems lies with the research biologist studying behaviour and physiology. Recent findings in this sphere have been significant and there is some basis for optimism that they will lead eventually to much more successful design of apparatus for directing salmon from the broad expanse of turbulent spill into the fish facilities. None of these developments have reached the stage where a solution based on them could be considered a calculated risk in a mammoth application to the Fraser.
I interject at this time, Mr. Speaker, because the hon. member for Coast-Capilano made some brief reference to the research facilities. While I was a member of the fisheries committee 1 took the opportunity to ask Dr. Pritchard whether there was sufficient money and men available to do the necessary research to try to solve the problem. He explained to me the problem was not one of the number of men. He said that at the present time they have approximately 75 scientists and engineers working on this fish-power problem. There is a joint outlay between Canada and the United States of approximately $3 million every year on this problem.
Returning to the article, I find it states:
The second problem is centred on the safe transport of hundreds of millions of young fish down over spillways and through turbines. A large and well co-ordinated research effort has gone into both the design of spillways and turbines to minimize losses, and engineering and biological studies to probe the possibilities of directing or guiding the young fish into safe downstream bypasses. Where river flow is extremely small, guiding by electricity or light has been used with success. In small 66968-9-227
Fraser River Fisheries
forebay installations mechanical screening may be a feasible though costly protection. None of these techniques has measured up to the problem posed by large mainstem developments in which the freshet discharge accompanies the downstream navigation of the fish. For instance, effective mechanical screening on the Fraser would necessitate maintenance of approach velocities of less than 1 foot per second in the forebay of dams which with existing design would have velocities of 13 feet per second during freshet periods. It is obvious that in addition to the tremendous costs of screening, physical conditions in the Fraser canyon make it impossible to meet such standards.
I might say, Mr. Speaker, both the fisheries association and the united fishermen and allied workers union have opposed power development on the Fraser river. Although both organizations recognize the need for flood control they have steadfastly been in agreement that power dams should not be erected on the Fraser river. This is one of the few occasions on which they have been in agreement. I must commend the hon. member for Victoria, B.C. for bringing forward this legislation although I must reiterate that, as for myself, I do not feel that it goes sufficiently far.

Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to take up much of the time of the house on this bill. It has been fairly well explained pro and con by the hon. member for Coast-Capilano (Mr. Payne) and the hon. member for Bur-naby-Richmond (Mr. Drysdale). I should like to thank the hon. member for Victoria, B.C. (Mr. McPhillips) for his interest in the Fraser river and to congratulate him on bringing forward his bill.
As all hon. members of this house know, the Fraser river is the greatest salmon river in the world, as was pointed out by the hon. member for Victoria, B.C. From experience we all know what the power dams on the lower Columbia river did to the salmon runs of that great river. We also know that the United States government has spent hundreds of millions of dollars in trying to bring back the salmon runs of the Columbia river but has met with little success.
I understand that the value of the fish pack from the Fraser river run last year was between $80 million and $100 million. That resource has added a terrific amount to the economy of the province of British Columbia. It is not altogether the monetary value which we are considering when we think of the fish; it is the great food value that will eventually be lost if that salmon run of which we are so proud is ever decimated. With the development of the upper Columbia river and with the power potentials of the Peace and other non-fish bearing rivers of British Columbia, I believe we shall have for many years all the power that we need in our

Fraser River Fisheries
province. With the great development of atomic energy and nuclear power I think the time may be near when the need for development of the Fraser river for power will be past and that we shall have plenty of power and also the fish produced in that great river.
I am convinced the time lies a long way in the future when we can have both fish and power. From all the experiments that have gone on in the past, there is no sign that we can have both on this great river.

maintopic: LEGISLATION TO SAFEGUARD NAVIGATION AND FISHERIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Fraser river is about three miles from my constituency but in my riding I have a great number of fishermen. On behalf of myself and the fishermen of my riding I can say that we appreciate the interest of the hon. member for Victoria, B.C. (Mr. Mc-Phillips) on Vancouver island some 75 miles away, in the maintenance of the fishing industry in general and the salmon industry in particular on the Fraser river. However, I want to say this most emphatically, and I think I understand the problems of the fishermen and the importance of the Fraser river. I want to say that I cannot agree with the terms set forth in Bill No. C-23. Clause 1, without any question of doubt whatsoever -and here I completely agree with the remarks made by the hon. member for Coast-Capilano (Mr. Payne)-completely slams the door on any development whatsoever of the Fraser river because it contains this provision:
1. No hydroelectric power shall be generated in the Fraser river in the province of British Columbia, nor shall any dam, weir or other obstruction to navigation or to the spawning run of the Pacific salmon, be constructed in or over the said river.
I am afraid that the hon. member for Victoria (B.C.) does not understand the development and the resources of the Fraser river. It was not too many years ago that nature itself, by means of land slides, almost completely obstructed the Fraser river in what is known as Hells canyon or Hells Gate. What happened? The federal government of that day spent a great deal of money in the construction of a fish ladder at Hells canyon. I think it cost in the neighbourhood of $1J million, although I may be wrong in the figure. From the hon. member who just sat down, Mr. Speaker, you heard about the Adams river run which is of only a certain type of salmon. There are four species that go up the Fraser river. This year the greatest run that British Columbia has ever known on the Fraser river, on the Adams river run, got over what? It did not get through Hells Gate directly but it got through the fish ladder constructed at Hells canyon or what is known as Hells Gate.

According to reports millions of fish died because there were so many. There was there, as there is now, complete proof that when nature caused an obstruction and when a government took action of a scientific nature, the run was not only maintained but was of such a nature that millions of fish, when they reached their spawning ground, died in large numbers. I saw pictures of them only the other week. You could almost walk over their bodies on the Adams river.
In addition to that, as I say, with the principle and purpose of this bill I completely agree. However, it closes the door to scientific knowledge and proof by the federal government, even up to now, that at Hells Gate you can take care of the fish.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE RATES OF REMUNERATION AND CONTRIBUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill is to increase the contributions made to the unemployment insurance fund by the government, the employers, the employees and by those who will benefit under this measure. In other words, it is sought by means of this legislation to increase the rates of contribution by the employer and the employee by about 30 per cent without at the same time increasing the benefits to the employee.
For every dollar put into the fund before this measure was brought before the house, 40 cents thereof was paid each week by the employer, 40 cents by the employee and 20 cents by the government. This contribution will hereafter amount to 52 cents from the employer, 52 cents from the employee and 26 cents from the government. Why has it been found necessary to do this? The minister, in introducing this measure, stated in effect that it was because the fund is depleting. The hon. minister said this was required in order to maintain the fund in a stable position during the next two years.

During the last two years of recession the minister has indicated that there has been a heavy payment out of the fund. He has stated, further, that it is the responsibility of the government to see to it that this fund is able to meet whatever eventualities may arise. But I say to him that it is also the responsibility of the government to protect the fund. The government did not discharge that responsibility, and because it did not discharge that responsibility it is now asking the employer and the employee to pay the shot by means of this measure.
This, sir, is just another tax; it is just another method of imposing taxes on the people of this country which should have been announced during the budget debate. This, I say, is another way-a backdoor method, if you will-of collecting taxes. By means of this additional tax to which no reference was made in the budget speech It is expected to raise between $80 million and $100 million over a period of one year. That is a substantial sum of money having regard to the increased taxation which has already been placed upon the people of Canada.
I say that the unemployment insurance fund has not been properly administered. Last year the fund suffered a loss of $10 million in the sale of securities. According to sessional paper 82A which was tabled in the house it appears that the fund held about $400 million in victory bonds and we have good reason to believe that a substantial portion of those bonds were conveited. Later when cash was required to meet the calls made upon the insurance fund by the unemployed, the government was forced to sell government securities, and as a result of these operations it made a loss exceeding $10 million. The administration of this fund is an example of how the conversion loan worked out. The government lost this money and it is now calling upon the workers to pay a portion of the bill.
What are the facts? The facts are contained in a document known as sessional paper 82A. I will not repeat what was said last night by the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin), but there are a number of things which I believe should be drawn to the attention of the house and which are to be found in this document. As of March 31, 1958 the balance to the credit of the unemployment insurance fund was $744 million, approximately, which was a decrease of $134 million over the 12 months period. The revenue for the fiscal year 1957-58 totalled $250 million, roughly, and benefits paid in the year 1957-1958 totalled $385 million. This represents an increase over the previous year of $153 million in total benefits. The operations of the year 66968-9-227i
Unemployment Insurance Act resulted in an excess of expenditure over revenue of $134 million. I think it is important that this should be brought to the attention of the house, because repeatedly, not only in this report which I hold in my hand but also in the other report of August 26 which was tabled yesterday by the minister, there is reference to this drain upon the unemployment insurance fund. Here it is stated that the staggering increase in benefit payments is mainly due to the large number of unemployed workers during the period and to the extension of the period during which seasonal benefits were available.
There are at this time 525,000 unemployed persons seeking jobs in this country, and more than one-third of those are in the province of Quebec. In the province of Quebec alone that represents 12.5 per cent of the working force, and I remind the minister that it is because of this unemployment that the drain on the fund which is referred to in this and in the other report is mentioned by the advisory committee.
The advisory committee also calls attention to the serious situation in which the fund finds itself. "It is a fact, however," states the committee, "that the burden of this expense, in the opinion of the committee, should not be imposed on the unemployment insurance fund unless the loss to the fund is made good." The committee goes on to state:
We trust the government will take action to replace the drain on the fund, by reason of the extension of the seasonal benefit period by a grant.

The committee respectfully recommends that the division of responsibility for revenue to the fund as between employers, employees and government be adjusted so that the contribution from each be made equal. In the meantime we respectfully draw your attention to our report of July 18, 1958.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE RATES OF REMUNERATION AND CONTRIBUTIONS, ETC.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, there is a slightly different point actually, it seems to me, that the hon. member for Laurier was trying to make. Your Honour will recall that, according to May's sixteenth edition, it is competent to members to move amendments which may express opinions as to any circumstances connected with the introduction or prosecution of a bill. speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE RATES OF REMUNERATION AND CONTRIBUTIONS, ETC.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE RATES OF REMUNERATION AND CONTRIBUTIONS, ETC.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE RATES OF REMUNERATION AND CONTRIBUTIONS, ETC.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE RATES OF REMUNERATION AND CONTRIBUTIONS, ETC.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE RATES OF REMUNERATION AND CONTRIBUTIONS, ETC.

This is the second reading of a bill to amend an act. It has been very well established, and the practice has been very closely followed in the house, that a bill to amend a particular act opens up only the sections that it seeks to amend. Now, there are three or four principles or purposes in those amendments: one has to do with the numbers who may benefit; one has to do with the amount of benefits; one has to do with the amount of contributions. That is a fairly broad range of the unemployment insurance scheme, but it does not open up the whole act by any means, and it does not open up debate on the contents of the Unemployment Insurance Act, the advisory committee and its relations with the government.
[The Speaker.!

It only opens up the principles which I think were reasonably correctly stated, as I understand the bill, by the minister when he introduced the bill yesterday and referred to the four principal changes which are the purposes and principles of the bill.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE RATES OF REMUNERATION AND CONTRIBUTIONS, ETC.

I asked the unemployment insurance advisory committee to give some study to some of my suggestions for amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act, which they did.
The minister said in this statement which I have just read that the report was given to him at his request; that he asked the unemployment insurance advisory committee to give some study to some of his suggestions, which they did. He considered the report as confidential but the report which was tabled yesterday is not so marked. subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE RATES OF REMUNERATION AND CONTRIBUTIONS, ETC.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE RATES OF REMUNERATION AND CONTRIBUTIONS, ETC.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE RATES OF REMUNERATION AND CONTRIBUTIONS, ETC.

Why is it, that in the last part of this report there is not only no indication that the minister asked for suggestions but on the contrary there seems to be clear-cut
Unemployment Insurance Act evidence, and it appears from the last paragraph, that although at least three members of the advisory committee were not in accord with the minister, the minister had not notified the committee of his intentions. The minister says that he asked the advisory committee to study some of his suggestions for amendments to the act. I say, that the minister has no right to do that. Section 91 (1) of the act reads as follows:
Whenever the governor in council, after consultation with the commission, considers it expedient to do so, he may direct the advisory committee to investigate and to report upon,
(a)	the provision of unemployment insurance-
(b)	the rates of contribution and benefit-
Parliament has not given the minister the power to ask for the report which he said he asked for. The minister took that power and he had no right to take that power. The minister acted in contravention of the Unemployment Insurance Act. I say that the minister should explain to the house why and under what authority he did ask for this report because I have been unable to find anywhere in the act any statutory authority that gives the minister jurisdiction to ask for a report of this kind. Unemployment Insurance Act

In
an effort to regain my temporary ascendancy as the acting leader of this law abiding parliamentary group, I wish to make a few general remarks. I am not going to be repetitious, and I am not going to be verbose. Our views and criticisms with respect to this bill were ably placed before the house by the very good-looking member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) and the equally good-looking member for Skeena (Mr. Howard).
I discussed this unemployment insurance legislation with a number of my constituents. They were very interested in the operation of the act, and very interested in amendments which were even then, as it were, in the air. I must say before I proceed that I find it somewhat difficult to work up a suitable political head of steam when I look at the genial and very much respected Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr). I may say that we in this group do not blame him entirely for the deficiencies of this bill. The hon. gentleman is one of a

Unemployment Insurance Act cabinet. We are of the opinion that if he had had his own way all the amendments which the official opposition and we in this group are proposing would have been already incorporated in this measure.
The Unemployment Insurance Act is a very sound piece of legislation, and one which has been of great benefit to hundreds of thousands of Canadians. I think we are sometimes inclined to overlook the days when there was no Unemployment Insurance Act and when people who, for one reason or another, lost their employment were obliged to rush around for a few extra dollars or go on relief. This legislation represented a big step forward. I do want to remind the house that this legislation was placed on the statute books of this country after men like Mr. J. S. Woodsworth and Mr. William Irvine had urged the government of that day year after year to make provision of this kind. I think when we are discussing this legislation we should not fail to remind ourselves of the pioneer work done in this respect by former members of the C.C.F. party in this house-

speechtext: And Liberals, too.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE RATES OF REMUNERATION AND CONTRIBUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: Yes, and by some other hon. members of that day. There were a few of the more progressive Liberals who supported us in those efforts.

speechtext: New leader.

I see that hon. members are trying to interrupt me.
While these good people of the past-members of this house, representatives of the labour movement, and people in other sections of our society-were urging the adoption of this type of legislation, there were other people who strongly objected to it. I am sure there are members of this house who remember the heated criticism made by some Tory-minded people of that day.

speechtext: We have them right in this house, too.

The hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) is correct. I am not suggesting that they were all members of the Progressive Conservative party, but there were some Tory-minded members of this house, and some members of the other place, too, who regarded this legislation as a dole rather than as legislation based on the principle of insurance in order to provide against days of adversity.
Experience in changing circumstances has clearly demonstrated the necessity for periodical amendments to this act. This is one of the times when amendments are indicated and justified. While there are some improvements in the measure, some things which

this group welcomes, there are also reasons for disappointment because of the omission of certain things which this group thinks should have been in the bill before us at the present time.
The extension of the benefit to 52 weeks is excellent, and we support that wholeheartedly. The protection of people earning up to $5,460 is also an excellent amendment. There is also some improvement in the rates of benefit; not as much as we should like to see, but some improvement. Higher earnings are also permitted for certain persons before they are considered ineligible for benefits and this, too, we consider to be an improvement because it provides an opportunity for exercising initiative and helping oneself while receiving unemployment insurance benefit. And then there is the question of extending the benefits to persons who are in a penitentiary for up to two years. That is an excellent improvement.
We support the protest made by many hon. members at the use of the greater portion of the increased contribution for the rebuilding of the capital of the fund. We think that is most unsound in principle. We think it is a decided departure from the insurance principle upon which the act is based. We have been informed that only 1 per cent of the 80 per cent increase expected is required to pay for the extension of benefits up to 52 weeks, and that the balance will largely be used to rebuild the capital of the fund. When the minister replies before the conclusion of this debate on second reading I hope he will give the house some figures in this connection. I repeat, that we have been informed that it only requires 1 per cent of the 30 per cent increase expected to meet the cost of the increased benefits and that the balance will be used largely to rebuild the capital of the fund. I hope the minister will give us some figures in this connection in order that we may know whether we are dealing with facts. We want to be accurate in this respect, because to criticize on unfair or incorrect facts is only to render invalid the argument one is trying to make.
I want to deal with three omissions from the bill from our point of view, three things which we regret have not been included in this measure. I intend to be quite brief. First, we regret that while the minister was amending this act provision was not made for the inclusion of farm labourers. This question has been discussed repeatedly in the house, and I know that there are a goodly number of members who support the government at the present time and who, when

they were in opposition, felt that the government of the day should include farm labourers under the provisions of the Unemployment Insurance Act. We are very sorry they have not been included, because it is most unfair to the farmers of the country. I am repeatedly having farmers come to me and say how difficult it is for them to get labour on the farms because, naturally, men prefer to seek employment in fields where they have the protection of the Unemployment Insurance Act; they are not anxious to work for a farmer for two or three weeks if they are not to have the benefit of this protection. I shall have more to say on this subject when the estimates of the Department of Labour come before us for consideration. I think there will have to be a much more accurate definition as to what exactly a farm labourer is. I was talking to the local manager of the unemployment service-
Surely I am not out of order, Mr. Speaker?

Unemployment Insurance Act
As the final paragraph of my recitation I would say I think some consideration should be given to bringing under the terms of the Unemployment Insurance Act members of the armed forces who are on short term service. It has been brought to my attention and to the attention of other hon. members in this group that men who are in the armed forces for short periods up to five years and are then discharged, as men were within the last year or eighteen months owing to the recession and lack of employment, have found themselves unemployed and without any unemployment insurance protection. We think that men who have joined the armed forces and served their country should receive on their discharge the protection of unemployment insurance.
We would urge consideration of an amendment to protect those persons discharged from the armed forces of Canada. I know there is some objection to that from the Department of National Defence. In an issue like this I do not think the decision should be left to the senior officers of the Department of National Defence. Senior officers have a prejudice about things like unemployment insurance. Some may even think it somewhat degrading. This decision should be made by the Department of Labour and this protection given to those young Canadians.
We in this group think the time is ripe for a thorough review of the Unemployment Insurance Act. We urge the minister to give consideration to our criticisms of the present bill and to our suggestion for the inclusion of other groups so we can build up in this country on the foundations already laid a complete, just and sound unemployment insurance system to protect those who suffer adversity through temporary unemployment. We cannot evade the fact that owing to our climate and other circumstances in the country with all the best arrangements there is bound to be a measure of seasonal unemployment in Canada. We must provide for that. We in this group believe in building up this act so it is based on sound insurance principles to cover those who pay for their own protection and in so doing provide for their own security.

I say that because of these transactions alone, that is one of the reasons -and I come back to that matter-that I am going to vote against this bill. I am giving the reasons why I am going to vote against this bill and this is one of them.
Another reason is that we have not before us the statutory report for the year ending March 31, 1959 on the fund itself. Surely on May 12 or at the date on which this measure was brought before us in the form of a resolution the least the government could have done was to give us the up to date information which the government is obliged by statute to do on the state of this fund. Here we are being asked-and this is certainly relevant to the bill-to put another tax on the producers of Canada, the workers and the manufacturers and other employers, to raise the cost of living in Canada; to raise the cost of production; to weaken our competitive position in world markets, because all these things flow from the increased imposts.
We are being asked to do this blindly and without the information to which we are entitled under the law, because the government chose to hide it from us when they found it embarrassing. It would have given a different appearance to the whole financial transactions, to the whole budget. One can understand why the minister did not want anyone to see these orders in council, did not want anyone to see how much confidence there was in their bonds, with the insistence on 105 per cent security and a 5 per cent rate. It is relevant because this charge is being imposed under the guise of insurance upon certain specific contributors, not upon the generality of taxpayers. The poor general taxpayer is obliged to pay and pay and pay for the pleasure of having the present Minister of Finance. But at least when it is straight taxation it is supposed to be imposed equitably on the whole body politic, and when we have good government it is so imposed. But here under the guise of insurance the contributors to the unemployment insurance fund-of whom I am not one but many of whom I represent are-are being asked to pay an additional tax to pay this interest rate to the minister. That is what is happening.
Surely it is a most elementary thing that the minister should rise in his place and tell us why, when there is some $400 million still in the fund in the form of bonds, it was necessary to make this loan at all at this high rate of interest. Why was not the fund managed in such a fashion that it was in a liquid state so that these loans would not be


necessary? As to 5 per cent on $80 million, I am not very good at mental arithmetic but I know it is a great deal of money. When the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Brunsden) talks about human relations and gives us this heart-bleeding stuff that we listened to from him, he should not forget that this is really a fraud being perpetrated on these people under the guide of insurance. That is what it is and the minister knows it perfectly well.

The other reason why I intend to vote against the bill is this. I must say I voted with more satisfaction for the amendment of the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin). If that proposition had not been decided in the negative, there would have been even greater force to my argument than there is now. But it is unfair, unreasonable and unjust to ask the insured contributors to pay for these welfare benefits that the Prime Minister described in his last television show as these payments that came from the government for human betterment. They did not come from the government at all. They came from the insurance fund which belongs to the people who are insured. It does not belong to the government.
It is true that this parliament passed these various statutes that were brought down one after another last year extending the period of seasonal benefits until the winter was extended into June. We all know that. On every occasion the hon. member for Essex East rose in his place in the house and appealed to the minister and to the Minister of Finance to do the honest thing. He said that we were in favour of these seasonal benefits but that they should be paid for out of the treasury, that they should not be charged against the fund because they were not actuarially sound, and everybody knows they are not. It is this extension of benefits that are not actuarially sound, paid for out of the payments that were made by those people who were under categories that were actuarially sound, that has created the difficulty which the minister is now proposing to ask parliament to cure by this method of increasing the contributions of the workers and the producers, with all the deleterious economic effects that will flow from it. It is imposing a special tax on a select group of people. That is all it is. In my opinion, that is an adequate reason for voting against this bill. But it is not the only reason for voting against this bill. There is another reason and it is this.
